blocks.text: By the Greek translators שלו selau is rendered not ὄρτυξ [ortyx] coturnix [quail], but ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] ortygometra. Thus Exod. XVI, 13. Ἀνέβη ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē ortygomētra]. And Num. XI, 31. Ἐξεπέρασεν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Exeperasen ortygomētran]. And in the following verse, Καὶ συνέλεγον τὴν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Kai synelegon tēn ortygomētran]. And Psal. CIV, 40. Ἤιτησαν, καὶ ἦλθεν ὀρτυγομήτρα [Ētēsan, kai ēlthen ortygomētra]. And Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Ἦλθε μάλ᾽ αἰτίζουσιν ἀπείριτος ὀρτυγομήτρα. [Ēlthe mal' aitizousin apeiritos ortygomētra.]

[II, 651] And Sap. XVI, 2. Τροφὴν ἡτοίμασας ὀρτυγομήτραν [Trophēn hētoimasas ortygomētran]. And Sap. XIX, 12. Ἀνέβη αὐτοῖς ἐκ θαλάσσης ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē autois ek thalassēs ortygomētra]. And Philo, book 1 On the Life of Moses, Ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος συνεχὲς ἐκ θαλάττης ἐπιφερόμενον πᾶν τὸ στρατόπεδον ἐπεσκίαζε [Ortygomētrōn nephos syneches ek thalattēs epipheromenon pan to stratopedon epeskiaze]. Nor are there lacking those to whom the ortygometra seems to be a bird different from the quail. Augustine on Exodus, Question 62: To them the ortygometra was given, that is, birds which many Latin translators have rendered quails, although the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. And long before, the Philosopher, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ὅταν δ' ἐντεῦθεν ἀπάρωσιν (οἱ ὄρτυγες) ἥ τε γλωττὶς συναπαίρει, καὶ ἡ ὀρτυγομήτρα, καὶ ὁ ὠτὸς, καὶ ὁ κύγχραμος [Hotan d' enteuthen aparōsin (hoi ortyges) hē te glōttis synapairei, kai hē ortygomētra, kai ho ōtos, kai ho kynchramos]· When they (the quails) depart from here, the lingulaca departs together with them, and the ortygometra, and the otus, and the cynchramus. From these words it is evident that the ortygometra, like the lingulaca, the otus and the cynchramus, is distinguished from the quail. Accordingly, further on in the same place there follows: Ἡ δὲ ὀρτυγομήτρα παραπλήσιος τὴν μορφὴν τοῖς λιμναίοις ἐστὶ [Hē de ortygomētra paraplēsios tēn morphēn tois limnaiois esti]· The ortygometra is similar in form to the marsh birds. And in Athenaeus, book 9, the same bird is described by Alexander of Myndus as τὸ μέγεθος ἡ λίκη τρυγὼν, σκέλη δὲ μακρὰ, δυσθαλπὴς καὶ δειλὴ [to megethos hē likē trygōn, skelē de makra, dysthalpēs kai deilē], of the size of a turtle-dove, with long legs, sensitive to cold and timid. Δυσθαλὴς [Dysthalēs], that is, ill-flourishing, is written there without any sense; but I have emended it to δυσθαλπής [dysthalpēs]. In the opinion of these authors, then, it is plain that the ortygometra differs in species from the quail ^{(3)}. For Hesychius, however, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] is nothing other than ὄρτυξ ὑπερμεγέθης [ortyx hypermegethēs], a very large quail, as if the mother or matrix of the others. So among cicadas there is the τεττιγομήτρα [tettigomētra], among sea-urchins the ἐχινομήτρα [echinomētra], among worms the ἰουλομήτρα [ioulomētra] (in Hesychius written ἰουλυμήτρα [ioulymētra]), among the species of lotus Pliny's λωτομήτρα [lōtomētra], and among cities and villages μητρόπολις [mētropolis] and μητροκωμία [mētrokōmia]. For Jansenius, on the book of Wisdom, ch. 16, gravely errs in holding that the ortygometra is so called as if μέτρον τῆς ὄρτυγος [metron tēs ortygos], as though it were the measure and regulator of the other quails. For the word is not written with ε, ὀρτυγόμετρα [ortygometra], but with η, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra], so that it plainly means what we said: mother or matrix of quails. And even from this you may infer that the ortygometra differs from the common quail only in size. Therefore many use ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] and coturnix [quail] indiscriminately. Among them is Josephus, who instead of ortygometras has simply ὀρτύγων πλῆθος [ortygōn plēthos], an abundance of quails, book 3, ch. 1. And again in ch. 12: Πίμπλαται τὸ στρατόπεδον ὀρτύγων ἅπαν [Pimplatai to stratopedon ortygōn hapan], The whole camp is filled with quails. Jerome too, who for the word ortygometra, which he retained in the Psalms and in the book of Wisdom, has coturnices [quails] in the Law. And the author of the Mirabilia, among the works of Augustine, book 1, ch. 27, [II, 652] plainly treats these as synonyms when he writes of this miracle: A wind, going forth from the Lord, seized quails across the sea and carried them to the places of the camp. And a little [col. 94] later: Around the places of the camp it set down the ortygometra. Nor was the intention of Aristophanes any different in the Birds, where he would have vows made

to Latona the ortygometra, that is, the quail. For Latona, when about to give birth, is fabled to have come to Delos changed into a quail, and the island was therefore called Ortygia, as if the quail's island. Jupiter too is fabled to have lain with her ὄρτυγι εἰκασθείς [ortygi eikastheis]. So the Scholiast on Pindar has it, in the argument of the Pythians. That Pliny and Solinus also counted the ortygometra among the kind of quails is proved by a great man in the Plinianae Exercitationes, p. 182. Nor do I doubt that the same was the view of the Greek translators, of the author of the book of Wisdom, of Philo and of Apollinaris, for whom שלו selau is ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra]. They preferred this word, however, to the simple ὄρτυξ [ortyx], lest it be thought that God had sent the Israelites common quails, rather than the noblest of them.
